passage:
Age ten: at his cousin's wedding, Naveen watched relatives swarm around his uncle, a senior officer, offering him the best chair and asking his opinion on everything. His own father, a tailor who had stitched half the wedding outfits, stood near the buffet and was nodded at once. Naveen frowned into his plate. 'Why don't they talk to Papa?' he whispered to his mother, Avni. She crouched down. 'Because they see the chair, not the man. Papa's hands made the dress you are wearing. Honest work has its own dignity, beta.' Naveen straightened up and went to stand beside his father.

Age twenty-five: Naveen, now a junior analyst, watched the team lead Charu present a plan on the screen. 'Tell me where this is weak,' she said. Nobody moved. Then Naveen raised a hand and pointed out that the figures in the third table used last year's rate. Charu looked at the page, then at him. 'You're right, I had missed that. Thank you for saying so in front of everyone.' She fixed it on the spot, and two others began raising their own doubts.

qa.q: What work does Naveen's father do?
qa.a: He is a tailor who stitched half the wedding outfits.

qa.q: How do Naveen's two experiences show different sides of rank at work?
qa.a: At ten he saw rank shape how relatives treated his officer uncle and his tailor father, and heard from his mother that honest work has dignity. At twenty-five he saw a senior lead invite disagreement and thank a junior, which made speaking up feel safe.

qa.q: What was Naveen feeling as he whispered, 'Why don't they talk to Papa?'
qa.a: Hurt and puzzled on his father's behalf, as the frown into his plate shows.

qa.q: What could Naveen do if he becomes a team lead one day?
qa.a: Ask openly where a plan is weak, thank whoever points it out, and give every colleague the same respect whatever their job title.

grounding: A child sees rank valued over honest work, and later a junior sees a leader welcome disagreement, both observed from outside.
